history: Pyxis, the Compass, was invented by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille. He spent 1751–52 at the Cape of Good Hope cataloging nearly ten thousand southern stars, and filled the gaps between the old figures with 14 new constellations, almost all of them named for the instruments of science and navigation. This one first appeared on his chart published in 1756 as la Boussole, the mariner's magnetic compass. On the second edition in 1763 he gave it the Latin name Pixis Nautica, which was later shortened and respelled as Pyxis.

Its stars were not new. Ptolemy had catalogued the four that Lacaille labeled Alpha, Beta, Gamma and Delta as stars in the mast of the ship Argo. Johann Bayer had given them no Greek letters in 1603, and Lacaille took them for his compass. Because it sits beside the ship, Pyxis is often said to be a fourth piece of Argo Navis, but that is a mistake: Lacaille split Argo into [[con:Car|Carina]], [[con:Pup|Puppis]] and [[con:Vel|Vela]] only, and listed the Compass separately among his new inventions. The compass is also an anachronism aboard a Greek galley, since the magnetic compass was unknown to the ancient Greeks.

In 1844 the English astronomer John Herschel proposed abolishing Pyxis and returning its stars to the ship as a fourth section called Malus, the Mast. Francis Baily adopted Malus in his British Association Catalogue of 1845, but few followed, and Benjamin Gould restored Pyxis in his southern catalog of 1879. The German astronomer Johann Bode once wound another invention around it, the Log and Line, which has not survived.

overview: Pyxis is a ship's magnetic compass, placed by Lacaille beside the mast of the old ship Argo. It is small and faint, three 4th-magnitude stars in a short line, best on February to April evenings: low in the south from mid-northern latitudes, high overhead from the southern hemisphere.
howToFind: Look on evenings in March, when Pyxis is due south and about a fist and a half above the horizon. Find [[star:Alphard|Alphard]], the solitary orange star of Hydra, which lies a bit more than two fists below and to the right of Regulus. From Alphard go about two and a half fists down and a little to the right. There, in a dim region to the left of the Milky Way, is a short, nearly vertical line of three faint stars a little under one fist long: [[star:γ Pyx|Gamma Pyxidis]] at the top, [[star:α Pyx|Alpha]] in the middle and [[star:β Pyx|Beta]] at the bottom.

If you have an open southern horizon and have managed to find [[star:Naos|Naos]] in Puppis, Alpha Pyxidis is about one fist to its upper left. The stars are magnitude 3.7 to 4.0, so binoculars are needed from the city, and a dark site helps a great deal at this low altitude.
shape: A short, slightly bent line of three faint stars, a little under one fist long. Nothing about it suggests a compass. From a city it is invisible without binoculars; from a dark site with a clear southern horizon the little line is easy enough to pick out once you know where to look.

mainStars.note: The brightest star in the Compass at magnitude 3.7, a hot blue-white giant nearly 900 light-years away and many thousands of times more luminous than the Sun.
A yellow giant of magnitude 4.0 at the southern end of the line, about 420 light-years away.
An orange giant of magnitude 4.0 at the northern end of the line, about 207 light-years away.

notableObjects.note: A faint open cluster of the 8th magnitude close to the star Zeta Pyxidis. A small telescope shows a modest sprinkle of dim stars; the low altitude from mid-northern latitudes makes it a challenge there.

facts: Pyxis is short for Pyxis Nautica, the mariner's box, meaning a ship's compass. Do not confuse it with Circinus, the drawing compasses, another Lacaille constellation.

Pyxis contains T Pyxidis, a recurrent nova: a star that has flared up from obscurity several times since 1890, most recently in 2011. At its brightest it reaches about magnitude 6 to 7, within range of binoculars.
Chinese astronomers joined most of these stars with some in Antlia into Tianmiao, the Celestial Temple, dedicated to the emperor's ancestors.
